science.methodText: LightGBM trained on VIIRS fire detections across all of Türkiye (0.05° cells, 2021–2025): FWI and sub-indices with rolling means, distance to roads, settlements and farmland, cell fire history, land cover, elevation and slope. FWI caps the class, so a day with low fire weather can’t show extreme risk.

reports.title: Reports from the ground
reports.lede: Every report from across Türkiye, ranked so the most urgent and best-checked ones are on top.
reports.demoNote: The starting reports are examples for the demo. Reports you send from this device are added and ranked too.
howList: Urgency: what was seen (flames > smoke > spark > stubble > litter), the model’s fire risk at that spot, how close it is to a town, and how recent it is.
Verification: photo attached, photo GPS and time match, not a reposted image, AI smoke/fire check, reporter track record, other reports nearby, and satellite heat from NASA FIRMS.
Emergency = flames or smoke, at least ‘Likely real’, sent in the last 3 hours.
When the photo checker runs, its trust score (EXIF, repost check, smoke/fire detection, AI image audit, weather and satellite) replaces the website’s estimate.

tr.title: Red pine: Türkiye’s main fire tree
tr.simple: Its sticky resin and dry needles burn very hot.
tr.numLabel: of the land burned by 2021’s 30 biggest fires was pure red pine forest
tr.more: Red pine (kızılçam) fills the hot coast from the Aegean to the Mediterranean, where most fires start. After a fire its cones drop seeds and young trees grow back. That is bouncing back — not resisting fire.

tr.title: Black pine can’t bounce back
tr.simple: Its fires used to stay on the ground. Now they climb into the treetops, and the trees die for good.
tr.numLabel: of black pine forest in Türkiye
tr.more: In 2021 black pine made up 7.67% (12,811 ha) of the area burned by the biggest fires. It has no way to recover from crown fires, so burned stands don’t regrow on their own.

tr.title: Maquis is the ladder fire climbs
tr.simple: Low shrubs under the pines carry a ground fire up into the treetops.
tr.numLabel: of maquis — about 30% of Türkiye’s forest land
tr.more: Common maquis plants are kermes oak, rock rose (Cistus), strawberry tree, mastic (Pistacia lentiscus) and Phillyrea. Clearing them near roads and villages breaks the ladder.

tr.title: Thin twigs catch fire first
tr.simple: The thinner the twig, the faster it dries out and burns.
tr.more: Scientists sort a tree’s crown fuel by thickness. The very fine twigs (under 3 mm) carry flames fastest — that’s why a dry pine crown can go up in seconds.

tr.title: Not every forest burns the same
tr.simple: Open woods full of shrubs, thick pine stands, eucalyptus and broadleaf woods all behave differently in a fire.
tr.more: Eucalyptus leaves are full of oils and are extremely flammable. Broadleaf trees such as oak, carob and laurel are often planted at village edges as green fire breaks.

tr.title: Same-age pine rows = one big fuel bed
tr.simple: Huge plantations of one pine, all the same age, give fire a non-stop path.
tr.more: Large pine plantations across the Mediterranean created continuous, even-aged stands that raise flammability and fire hazard. Mixing species and ages breaks that path.

tr.title: Fire season is getting longer
tr.simple: Most fires happen from May to November — and risk now reaches into autumn and early spring.
tr.numLabel: of forest fires happen between May and November
tr.more: Experts warn that under dry, windy weather, fires can now start as early as March and April and keep going into October and November.

tr.title: Most of our forests are at risk
tr.simple: About two out of three hectares of forest are highly vulnerable to fire.
tr.numLabel: of Türkiye’s forests (about 15 million ha) are highly vulnerable
tr.more: That’s why daily risk maps and early reports from people on the ground matter so much.

id.title: Wet peat doesn’t burn. Drained peat does.
id.simple: Peat is old, soggy plant matter. Drain it and it dries like fuel — and can smoulder underground for weeks.
id.numLabel: of Indonesia’s peatland made more fire-prone by damage (Pantau Gambut estimate, 2026)
id.more: Peat fires make thick, smoky haze. Blocking drainage canals keeps peat wet so it can’t burn.

id.title: Fires burn the “in-between” land
id.simple: Most fires aren’t in forests or in plantations — they’re on cleared, drained land waiting to be planted.
id.numLabel: of the area burned in 2019 (seven provinces) was idle land
id.more: Only 3% of the burned land was inside oil palm plantations and 0.4% in acacia, rubber or rice fields. Fires set on plantations can spread easily into the dry idle land around them.

id.title: The 2013 Riau fires in one bar
id.simple: Most of the land that burned had already lost its forest.
id.numLabel: burned in one week in June 2013, 84% of it on peat
id.more: Of the already-deforested land that burned, 57% was scrub and bare soil, 31% young oil palm and 7% mature oil palm. The fires happened in a wetter-than-normal year, after just two dry months.

id.title: The pine that crossed the equator
id.simple: Sumatran pine (tusam) is Indonesia’s own pine — and like Türkiye’s pines, its resin-rich needles burn hot.
id.more: It is widely planted in Java and Sulawesi. One study suspects that resin-tapping holes and tree size may affect how intensely it burns.

id.title: 2026: fires moved to the dry east
id.simple: Dry savannas in Nusa Tenggara burned a lot this year.
id.numLabel: burned in Indonesia in January–June 2026 — Bali & Nusa Tenggara had 18.7%
id.more: Savanna is the cover that burns most in Nusa Tenggara. In Mutis forest, burned plots are dominated by fire-tolerant Eucalyptus urophylla.

id.title: Burn too often and the forest changes
id.simple: Repeated fires turn tall swamp forest into gelam thickets and grassland.
id.more: Gelam (Melaleuca cajuputi) survives fire, so after many burns it takes over — and the original swamp forest doesn’t come back.

id.title: The grass that keeps fire alive
id.simple: Alang-alang grass takes over burned land, then burns again and again.
id.more: Repeated fires remove plants taller than alang-alang (Imperata cylindrica), so the grass stays in charge and trees can’t return.
